pitch_detail.notes: The physical crux. An off-width to fist crack leads up and over a bulge, then a strenuous thin hand crack angles up and right to a small roof. Pull the roof into a short wide section, finish up a hand crack that narrows to fingers, and belay from bolts on a ledge.
Jam over a bulge into a finger crack, step right into a wide section, then follow a hand crack that thins to fingers up to a ledge with a three-bolt anchor. This pitch can be linked with the first.

The technical crux. Step right and jam thin cracks to a horizontal break, follow a sustained finger crack to a pod, then take finger and hand cracks up and left over a couple of bulges to a two-bolt ledge belay. A 0.5-size cam is the awkward size to have here.
Corner and ledges lead up and right on slightly sandy rock, then back left to a good ledge with a two-bolt anchor. A bolt protects the follower.

Two finishes. The regular left finish climbs a short corner, hand-traverses left to an off-width in a dihedral, then traverses left under a roof (about 5.7 and airy) to the summit. Use plenty of slings against rope drag, or split the pitch in two. The direct right finish climbs the corner and then face moves past four bolts at 5.11a.

rappel_detail.notes: The first rappel from the top skips the anchor at the base of the final pitch.
Continue down the route from anchor to anchor.
Continue down the route from anchor to anchor.
Final rappel to the ground. Four rappels were made on a single 70 m rope; double-rope descents of about two 60 m rappels are also described.

review.changed: Wrote five pitches from one detailed account; lengths and bolt counts omitted (only the direct finish has a count). Rappel table is deliberately sparse: only the first rappel's quirk and the count are stated, no station details or lengths.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 4 and descent says 'three rappels'; sources describe 4-5 pitches (regular finish may be split) and four single-rope rappels or two double-rope 60 m rappels.

pitch_detail.notes: Two pitches that combine into one lead of roughly 160 ft. The first bolt is about nine feet off the ground, so a stick-clip or boost is needed to reach it.
About 70 ft to a comfortable ledge, a usual place to stop for the night when fixing the lower pitches.
The Wrinkles. A series of pendulums out right and tension traverses back left; when good placements run out, move left. This is the hardest aid of the route.
A good crack leads through the arching roof.
Follow a crack to a short bolt ladder.
A left-facing corner with a few trickier moves, ending at a decent stance below the last aid pitch. Tricam placements between bolt ladders on the upper pitches have flared out and held poorly.
Continue up the corner system, then pendulum left into another corner. The pitch ends on a large, dirty, sandy, down-sloping ledge with loose material, so move carefully.
Free climb a low-angle chimney full of loose debris, then a chute of loose sand, rock and plant matter. The belay is at a pair of good trees.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches from the one page that lists them. Grades given only where it states them. The P7 tricam remark comes from a search snippet of a photo caption and is mildly hedged. No rappel table: the sources read did not state the descent, so none was invented.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.8 only; sources rate it C2 (one lists 5.7 C2). Stored row has no descent; one climber reported finishing in seven pitches with 60 m ropes by combining.

pitch_detail.notes: Free climbing onto a pedestal, a first pin, then more free climbing above a tied-off pin. Hanging belay about 140 ft up.
About 70 ft, mostly nailing up a rotten seam with knifeblades. Placements mostly need to be tied off.
Pin placements in mud; many inch-square holes take angle pitons, most tied off. Described as the hardest aid on the route.
Traverse right along a sloping mud shelf, clip a bolt, and move about 5 ft right to an overhanging chimney. A 2 inch angle, then aid and some free moves lead to a belay astride the ridge crest.
A flared, ugly crack up the crest, mostly aided but reported to go free at about 5.9+. Rest on a large ledge before this pitch if needed.
Pin behind the boulder known as the Duck, a sparsely protected traverse, then a short funky chimney at about 5.8. Ends at the usual bivy spot.
A2 nailing, then a six-bolt ladder that goes free at about 5.6 except for one overhang. Ends at an exposed 18 inch square platform with five bolts of uneven quality.
Bolts 6-8 ft apart climbed in aiders, with one or two 5.8 free moves and fixed half-inch angles. Becomes continuous aid, then a long wide crack with some free climbing through the summit overhang.
Easy ground to the summit block.

rappel_detail.notes: First of two rappels from the summit down to the base of the 5.8 chimney and platform below the Duck.
Second rappel to the chimney base and platform.
Three rappels go straight down the north face from the platform.
Final rappel to the ground. Ropes pick up sand and grit; anchors were not described and may have changed since the account.

review.changed: Used a single 1994 narrative for pitch notes; grades only where it states them. Fixed-gear details are old and may have changed. Rappel entries have no lengths or anchor types because none were stated.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 8 and grade '5.8 C2+'; sources describe nine pitches and 5.8 A2+. Stored row has no descent; a five-rappel descent is described.

pitch_detail.notes: Finger jams and stemming off the Lower Ramp, slippery when sun-baked so an early start helps. The first move off the ground is tricky but protectable. Build a gear belay at the pod or stance.

Traverse to the base of the Ruper crack, an off-width that needs a #4 Camalot at the start; side cracks higher up can be protected. A few strenuous moves make this the crux of the lower half, with good protection and a few old pins. The guidebook links the traverse and crack as one pitch, but some parties split it. Belay at the two-bolt anchor where Rover and Ruper meet. The Rover variation to the left is solid 5.9.
Traverse onto the Upper Ramp. The three pitches below the ramp make a possible bail point by rappel.
Longer, relaxed climbing ending on an exposed ledge.

The upper traverse, which many climbers find the crux. The rock changes to slick, dark red sandstone with some unreliable holds. Three fixed pins are present, some questionable; small cams (.5 and smaller) supplement them.
A last short pitch to the saddle. One short 5.8- move is guarded by two pins, one of which wiggles; the top-out is runout at about 5.5 and can be wet after rain or snow.

review.changed: Pitch numbering follows the six-pitch guidebook count loosely; sources disagree on where exact pitch breaks fall (the traverse and crack are combined by some). No grades or lengths except the ones stated. No rappel table: the descent is via Chockstone Chimney and Vertigo rappels / scrambling and is not described station by station.
review.other_findings: Area is stored as Tower One; overview describes Redgarden Wall's Lower and Upper Ramps. Note the stored area name should be checked, as the route is generally filed on Redgarden Wall.

pitch_detail.notes: Start a few metres right of the big boulder at the base of the buttress. Follow a low-angle crack with a tree growing from it across the face to a two-bolt anchor at the base of a short chimney with a 6-10 inch crack.
Climb the chimney (a #4 Camalot low, or a #2 higher), then the slab above past five bolts.

Step right to a crack, climb it about 20 ft, then step left onto a slab with three bolts. A 5.11 variation steps sharply left past two bolts into a water groove and past one more bolt before rejoining the slab.
Clip a bolt out left, go around the corner, and climb the slab past two bolts. The last stretch to the anchor is run out.
Clip the first bolt, climb right to the arete and past a couple of bolts, then make a long reach up and left to a ledge with a two-bolt anchor. Belaying here reduces rope drag.
Climb about 20 ft to the first bolt, traverse right about 15 ft to a hard-to-see bolt, and continue right over a ridge. The zig-zag line causes drag even with long draws.

The crux. Climb to a finger crack and undercling, clip a bolt, then work around to the steep right side underclinging and clipping about 11 bolts, then straight up. Easily aided, and some rate the hard section as aid-worthy.
Sustained climbing with nine or ten bolts, including a difficult step left into a water groove, then easier ground.
Slabs about 30 m up and left to a single bolt roughly 20 ft out left of the direct line, then up and right about 20 m to a new two-bolt anchor. Can be simul-climbed.
Continue up slab climbing past one bolt to a new two-bolt anchor.
No bolts and no gear. Ends at a large tree or the top of the cliff. Loose or damp lichen and snapping crystals demand focus.

rappel_detail.station: At the northeast corner of the formation, reached by hiking the summit slabs and ridge north. Build an anchor and belay down to the fixed station.
rappel_detail.notes: Downclimbing the slab solo is potentially fatal, so belay to the rap station.
hazards: slab downclimb to the station is unprotected

rappel_detail.station: Second bolted station below the first.

review.changed: Wrote from a single detailed pitch list; individual pitch grades appear only where stated. Per-pitch lengths were not given. Belays are semi-hanging in general; some old 1/4 inch bolts high on the wall.
review.other_findings: An alpine club report lists 11 pitches and 5.11d with the crux headwall on pitch 7 pre-protected by a ten-bolt ladder; stored 12 pitches and 5.12- match the other source. Pitch numbering in sources may differ by one.
